Exact symbolic tests of serial independence. Companion software to
E. Ashtari Nezhad, *Information Variance and Exact Symbolic Tests of Serial
Independence*. A Python version with the same functions and output is on PyPI
(`pip install ivserial`).

## 1. What the package does

`ivserial` tests whether a time series is a sequence of independent and
identically distributed (i.i.d.) values. The test is **rank based and exact**:
under independence its P-value is valid for every sample size and every
continuous distribution, with no model, bandwidth or tuning parameter to
choose. It reports

* the P-value of the proposed **combined test C** and of its two components:
  the **block statistic Q**, which sees dependence among several consecutive
  values, including dependence that is invisible in every pair, and the
  **portmanteau P2**, which looks at pairs at lags 1 and 2;
* **V-hat**, the strength of the dependence on a scale from 0 to 1 (the serial
  Cramér coefficient, which for pairs is Cramér's V), and **Gamma-hat**, the
  efficiency of the test;
* the **patterns** of consecutive values that occur unusually often or rarely,
  which show what kind of dependence is present;
* **sample size and power** calculations, and the explicit **null
  distribution** of Q.

## 2. Two ways to use it

* **The window (no programming).** `ivserial_app()` opens the graphical
  interface in the browser: open a CSV or Excel file, pick a column, press
  *Run test*. Sample-size planning, the null distribution and this guide are
  in their own tabs.
* **R code.** `serial_test(x)` in a script or at the console; suited to many
  series and to reproducible work.

Both use the same functions and give the same results: everything that can be
done in code can also be done in the window.

| Task | Window (`ivserial_app()`) | R |
|---|---|---|
| Test one series | Test tab, choose column, *Run test* | `serial_test(x)` |
| Screen many series | tick *test all columns* | `screen_series(data)` |
| Prices to log returns | *Transform: log returns* | `transform = "logdiff"` |
| Options (B, seed, m, d, level, lags, patterns) | option fields | arguments of `serial_test` |
| Save results | *Save report (.txt)*, *Save results (.csv)* | `capture.output(print(res))`, `as.data.frame(res)` |
| Sample size / power | Sample size & power tab | `required_sample_size`, `approximate_power`, `sample_size_table` |
| Default resolution for n | *Resolution for n* | `choose_resolution(n)` |
| Null distribution, critical values | Null distribution tab | `null_limit_summary`, `null_limit_sf`, `null_limit_quantile` |

## 3. Installation

You need R (free, from <https://cran.r-project.org>); RStudio is optional.
In R, install the package from GitHub:

```r
install.packages("remotes")                       # once
remotes::install_github("emaad7/ivserial-r")
```

or, from a downloaded source file, `install.packages("ivserial_1.0.1.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source")`.
For the window also install `shiny`, and for Excel files `readxl`:

```r
install.packages(c("shiny", "readxl"))
```

Then

```r
library(ivserial)
ivserial_app()          # the window
ivserial_guide()        # this guide in the browser (also vignette("ivserial"))
```

## 4. Preparing your data

* A **CSV**, **TXT** or **Excel** (.xlsx) file, or any numeric vector in R.
* **One series per column, rows in time order** (oldest first). A first row
  with names is optional; the delimiter and a decimal comma are detected;
  non-numeric columns such as dates are ignored; missing values are removed.
* At least 20 observations; several hundred give the most informative results.
* **Prices or returns?** The test is applied to the values you give it. For
  prices and other trending series use the **log returns** (or differences): a
  trending series is never i.i.d., and the test would only detect the trend.

The package contains the 20 daily exchange rates analysed in the paper, as
the data frame `exchange_rates` and as the file
`system.file("extdata", "exchange_rates.csv", package = "ivserial")`
(prices; use the log-return transform).

## 5. The window

`ivserial_app()` opens the window in the web browser (or in the RStudio
viewer). It has four tabs.

**Test.** *Browse* for your data file, or press *Use example data*. Choose the
series (column), or tick *test all columns* to screen every column at once
(with Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment). Choose the transform: none, differences,
or log returns (prices). Press *Run test*. *Save report (.txt)* saves the
report and *Save results (.csv)* one row of results per series. The options
can be left at their defaults: *B* = 9999 random permutations, block length
*m* and classes *d* chosen automatically (`auto`), level 0.05, portmanteau
with lags 1 and 2. Keep the **seed** fixed to make the P-values reproducible;
leave it blank for a random seed.

**Sample size & power.** Enter Gamma, or V (between 0 and 1) instead, tau,
*m*, *d*, the level and the target powers, then press *Required sample size*,
*Power for n* or *Resolution for n*. *Use last test* fills in the estimates of
the last test, for example on a pilot sample.

**Null distribution.** Enter *m*, *d* and, optionally, a value of Q, and press
*Compute*: the components, mean, variance and critical values of the limit,
and the asymptotic P-value of Q.

**User guide.** This guide.

To finish, close the browser tab and press *Esc* (or *Stop*) in R.

## 6. R code

```{r}
library(ivserial)
x <- 100 * diff(log(exchange_rates$China))   # log returns of the yuan
res <- serial_test(x, B = 999, seed = 1, label = "China")
res
```

(The examples in this guide use `B = 999` to run quickly; the default is
`B = 9999`.) The result is a list:

```{r}
res$p_C                                  # P-value of the combined test C
res$reject                               # decision at level alpha
c(res$p_Q, res$p_P2, res$p_Q_asymptotic) # components, asymptotic P-value of Q
res$cramer_v                             # strength of dependence, 0 to 1
c(res$gamma_hat, res$tau_hat)            # efficiency and its standard deviation
head(res$cells, 4)                       # most over- and under-represented patterns
as.data.frame(res)[, c("label", "n", "p_C", "cramer_v")]   # one row of results
```

Options and prices:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
serial_test(exchange_rates$Japan, transform = "logdiff", label = "Japan")  # prices -> log returns
serial_test(x, m = 3, d = 4, lags = 3, B = 99999, alpha = 0.01)           # options
```

Reading a file and screening several series, with P-values adjusted for
multiple testing (Benjamini–Hochberg):

```{r}
fx <- read_series(system.file("extdata", "exchange_rates.csv", package = "ivserial"))
sc <- screen_series(fx[, c("China", "India", "Japan", "Euro")], transform = "logdiff",
                    B = 999, seed = 1)
sc
```

`sc$results` holds the individual results and `summary(sc)` prints every
report.

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `serial_test(x, m, d, d2, lags, B, seed, alpha, transform, label, n_cells)` | the test |
| `screen_series(data, columns, ...)` | many series, Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment |
| `required_sample_size(gamma, m, d, alpha, power, tau)` | observations needed for a given power |
| `approximate_power(gamma, n, m, d, alpha, tau)` | power for n observations |
| `sample_size_table(gamma, m, d, alpha, tau, power)` | sample sizes for several powers |
| `serial_cramer_v(gamma, m, d)`, `gamma_from_cramer_v(v, m, d)` | convert between Gamma and V |
| `choose_resolution(n)` | default (m, d) |
| `null_limit_summary(m, d)`, `null_limit_sf(q, m, d)`, `null_limit_quantile(alpha, m, d)` | null limit: moments, critical values, P-values |
| `read_series(path)` | numeric columns of a CSV, TXT or Excel file |
| `ivserial_app()` | the window |
| `ivserial_guide()` | this guide in the browser |

## 7. Reading the output

* **C** is the test to use. A P-value below the level (e.g. 0.05) rejects
  serial independence: the series has dependence that an i.i.d. sequence
  would not show.
* **Q** looks at blocks of *m* consecutive values and **P2** at pairs at lags 1
  and 2; C combines them exactly.
* **permutation / asymptotic.** Permutation P-values are exact; asymptotic ones
  use the explicit limits and are accurate for n ≥ 350.
* **V-hat** is the strength of dependence between 0 and 1 (serial Cramér
  coefficient): 0 means that blocks of *m* consecutive classes are
  independent, 1 that the class of any one value determines its whole block.
  For *m* = 2 it is Cramér's V of consecutive classes. Compare values at the
  same (*m*, *d*).
* **Gamma-hat** is the efficiency: the normalized information variance, the
  approximate Bahadur slope of the test; Gamma = (d^(m−1) − 1)·V². It drives
  the sample-size calculation and is about 0 under independence.
* **Patterns.** Each value is assigned to one of *d* classes by its rank
  (1 = lowest, *d* = highest). Residual = (observed − expected)/√expected;
  |residual| > 3 is notable. For the yuan, the pattern 3-3-3 occurs 41 times
  against 7.5 expected (residual 12.2): runs of near-zero changes around the
  official reference rate. The patterns 1-5-5, 1-1-5 and 5-5-5, made of large
  moves of either sign, reflect volatility clustering.

A rejection means that the values are not i.i.d. The patterns indicate the
kind of dependence, not a particular model.

## 8. Sample size and power

Gamma is the efficiency of the test (its approximate Bahadur slope), so it
converts directly into a sample size (Corollary 4.8 of the paper):

power ≈ Φ( (K·Gamma + μ₀ − q_α) / √(K·tau² + V₀) ),  K = n − m + 1,

where μ₀, V₀ and q_α are the mean, variance and upper α point of the null
limit. `serial_test` estimates both Gamma and tau from the data, so a pilot
sample or a comparable series gives a realistic plan. With tau = 0 the
formula is accurate for weak dependence and otherwise optimistic.

```{r}
approximate_power(0.13, n = 350, m = 3, d = 4, tau = 1.13)  # ARCH(1); simulated: 0.82
sample_size_table(0.13, m = 3, d = 4, tau = 1.13)
required_sample_size(gamma_from_cramer_v(0.1, 3, 4), m = 3, d = 4, tau = 1)  # from V
choose_resolution(350)
```

From a pilot sample:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
r <- serial_test(pilot, seed = 1)
required_sample_size(r$gamma_hat, r$m, r$d, power = 0.8, tau = r$tau_hat)
```

## 9. The null distribution

Under independence Q converges to
L(m, d) = Σ_{s=2}^{m} (m − s + 1) χ²((d−1)² d^(s−2)) (Theorem 4.1 of the paper):

```{r}
null_limit_summary(3, 4)
null_limit_sf(80, m = 3, d = 4)        # asymptotic P-value of Q = 80
```

## 10. Residuals of fitted models

The test can be applied to residuals, for example of an ARMA or standardized
GARCH model, to check whether dependence remains. The P-values are then only
approximately exact. When the model is estimated efficiently (maximum
likelihood with the correct innovation distribution) they remain valid and
are slightly conservative (Theorem 4.11 of the paper). After Gaussian
quasi-maximum likelihood with non-normal innovations they can be misleading,
especially for squared residuals; then use a model-based bootstrap: simulate
from the fitted model, re-estimate, and recompute the statistic (Section 4.5
of the paper).

```{r}
set.seed(3)
y <- arima.sim(list(ar = 0.5), n = 500)
fit <- arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0))
serial_test(residuals(fit), B = 999, seed = 1)$p_C
```

## 11. Troubleshooting

| Message | Solution |
|---|---|
| `there is no package called 'shiny'` | `install.packages("shiny")` |
| Excel file cannot be read | `install.packages("readxl")` |
| `install_github` fails | `install.packages("remotes")` first; or install from the downloaded `.tar.gz` file |
| "only ... blocks per pattern" | The series is short for the chosen (m, d); use the automatic choice or smaller values. |
| "at least 20 observations are needed" | The series (after removing missing values and differencing) is too short. |

## 12. Reference and citation

Default resolution: (m, d) = (3, 3) for n < 300, (3, ⌊(n−300)/400⌋+4) for
300 ≤ n < 1500, and m = ⌊log n/(2 log 3)⌋, d = 3 beyond; portmanteau classes
3, 4 or 5. Ties are broken at random, which keeps the test exact.
P-value = (1 + #{permuted statistics ≥ observed})/(B + 1). Computing time:
about 1.5 seconds for n = 1000 with B = 9999.

If you use the package, please cite the paper; `citation("ivserial")` gives
the reference. Source code and bug reports:
<https://github.com/emaad7/ivserial-r>. License: MIT.
